title: Exonerated Isn't the Same as Compensated
hook: Getting a conviction thrown out does not get you paid. In most states you must then prove your innocence all over again — to a higher standard, against a state that may still call you guilty.
key_points: Thirty-nine states and Washington, DC have wrongful-conviction compensation programs; Louisiana created its fund in 2005.
Vacating a conviction is not enough: a claimant must separately establish factual innocence.
Louisiana requires 'clear and convincing' evidence of innocence, a higher bar than the 'preponderance' standard many states use.
Louisiana's statute contemplates a decision within five months and payment up to $480,000 — timelines are routinely exceeded.
Elvis Brooks served 42 years on a 1977 eyewitness conviction; a prosecutor later admitted withholding fingerprint evidence that did not match him.
The attorney general's office opposed 22 of 23 claims — far above a predecessor's roughly one-third rate.
content_html: There is a gap in the exoneration story that rarely makes the headlines. A court vacating a conviction says the conviction cannot stand; it does not say the person is innocent. Compensation is a separate proceeding with its own burden of proof, and in most states it is the claimant who carries it. ProPublica's reporting on Louisiana shows how wide that gap can get.
extra_html:
Thirty-nine states and the District of Columbia have compensation programs; Louisiana set its fund up in 2005, with awards up to $480,000 and a statutory expectation that claims be resolved within about five months — a deadline the reporting says is frequently blown. The distinguishing feature is the standard: applicants must show innocence by "clear and convincing" evidence, a level meant to leave little doubt in the judge's mind, rather than the "preponderance" standard (more likely than not) used in many states and in ordinary civil cases.

Elvis Brooks illustrates the stakes. He spent 42 years in prison on a 1977 murder conviction built on eyewitness identification, with no physical evidence tying him to the crime and twelve witnesses placing him elsewhere; fingerprints lifted from beer cans at the scene did not match him, and a prosecutor later admitted the fingerprint evidence had been withheld. His conviction was vacated in 2022, after he had already taken a plea in 2019. Attorney General Liz Murrill's office argued he should receive nothing, maintaining he is still guilty, and sought to reinstate a manslaughter charge. ProPublica puts that in context: Murrill's office has opposed 22 of 23 claims, where a predecessor opposed roughly a third and another former attorney general opposed 10 of 12 — a national expert told the outlet they could not think of a more aggressive record. The design lesson is generic to any compensation scheme: a right that requires you to defeat the government twice, on the government's terms, is worth much less than it looks on paper.

related.title: Junk Science & Wrongful Conviction
related.hook: A courtroom isn't a lab — but it has to rely on forensic science anyway. When that science turns out to be unreliable, the wrong person can spend years, or a life, on death row.

related.title: When DNA Evidence Outlasts the Statute of Limitations
related.hook: A crime can go unprosecuted forever once its statute of limitations runs out — even if DNA later identifies a suspect. Massachusetts is one of the last states moving to close that gap.

related.title: Due Process
related.hook: Due process is the promise that the state can't take your liberty or property on a whim — it must follow fair, known rules before it acts against you.

flashcards.prompt: Why can someone whose conviction was vacated still be denied compensation?
flashcards.back_html: Vacatur means the conviction cannot stand — not that innocence was proved. Compensation statutes require a separate showing of factual innocence, often to a demanding standard.

flashcards.prompt: How does Louisiana's evidentiary standard for compensation compare with many other states?

choices.text: It requires 'clear and convincing' evidence of innocence, higher than the 'preponderance' standard many states use
It requires proof beyond a reasonable doubt, the criminal standard
It requires no showing at all once a conviction is vacated

flashcards.explanation_html: Clear and convincing sits above preponderance (more likely than not) and below beyond a reasonable doubt — a meaningfully harder burden for the claimant to carry.

flashcards.prompt: What structural feature of these programs does the Brooks case expose?

choices.text: The same state that prosecuted the case gets to contest the compensation claim
Compensation is paid automatically by the federal government
Claims are decided by a jury of local residents

flashcards.explanation_html: The attorney general's office litigates against claimants — and can maintain a person is guilty even after a court has vacated the conviction.
